threads.thread_goal: Align on current loading, stacking and cleaning practices and main pain points.

messages.text:
Kickoff for the warehouse loading bay safety and efficiency upgrade project_title.
Can everyone share how we actually load, stack and clean today so we can map it for T1?
Quick prompts:
- For a standard mixed pallet truck, what steps do you follow from truck arrival to departure?
- How do you decide stacking order and weight distribution in practice?
- What gets cleaned between trucks and at end of shift, and who does it?
I will start pulling this into a draft map for T1 and later we can log issues in A5 during the pilot.
Please be concrete, including any shortcuts you see on the floor.

For a normal mixed pallet truck:
- Truck backs into bay, we usually skip a formal pre-check unless the floor looks really bad.
- I grab a forklift, quick look at pallet labels, then start with the heaviest pallets at the front of the trailer.
- I try to keep similar goods together but if we are in a rush I just fill gaps.
- For stacking, I mostly go by feel: heavy at the bottom, lighter on top, avoid leaning stacks.
Cleaning:
- If there is a spill, we throw some absorbent and sweep.
- End of shift, someone does a quick sweep around the dock, but it depends who has time.
Pain points: when we get dangerous goods or animal loads, I am never fully sure about the exact order, I just ask whoever seems to know.

On my side, for full pallet FMCG trucks:
- I check the delivery note and look at the route sequence if it is printed, but often it is not.
- I place the first drop pallets near the door so they come off first, but sometimes dispatch asks to change it last minute.
- Weight wise, I try to keep the center of gravity low and close to the trailer axles, but we do not have a clear rule posted.
Stacking:
- Max 3 layers on the weaker pallets, 4 on the stronger ones, based on what I have seen, not on a written rule.
Cleaning:
- We clear plastic wrap and broken wood when it starts to pile up, not on a fixed schedule.
Main issues: plastic wrap on the floor near the dock edge, and pallets left in the forklift path.

From the factory hand side:
- Between trucks we usually just move obvious obstacles out of the way so movers can keep loading.
- Proper sweeping of ramps and checking emergency exits tends to happen once per shift, often at the end.
- No formal checklist for floors, ramps, equipment, exits; it is more whoever notices something.
Pain points:
- Oil spots near the dock plates stay there too long.
- Some blind corners where forklifts and people cross without markings.
This will be useful input when we design the checklist for T4 and later the tracker in T11.

Adding what I see on raw materials trucks:
- For heavy raw materials, we often unload from the middle first if that is where the forklift can reach best, not always front to back.
- We sometimes double-stack pallets in the staging area to save space, even when the bottom pallet looks a bit tired.
- For cleaning, I usually sweep around the staging area when I have a gap, but there is no set time.
Biggest issues:
- Broken boards left on the floor.
- Shrink wrap tails getting caught under wheels.
- No clear rule on where to park empty pallets, so they end up near the dock edge.

Thanks, this helps for T1.
I am hearing a few patterns:
- Weight and stacking are mostly based on experience, not a posted rule.
- Cleaning is reactive, not on a fixed routine.
- Special loads like dangerous goods and animals are handled case by case.
To move forward, we need to pick which load types and routes we focus on first for mapping and later for the pilot.
My proposal:
1) Mixed pallet FMCG route with multiple drops.
2) Raw materials inbound route with heavy pallets.
3) One special load type, either dangerous goods or animals.
Can you all say which of these gives us the most impact if we start there?

For me, the mixed pallet FMCG with multiple drops is where we lose the most time.
We often reshuffle pallets at the first stop because the order is not right.
I would vote to start with that route and also include animals, since I handle those sometimes and I am never fully sure about the exact rules.
Raw materials are heavy but usually more straightforward once the forklift is in place.

I agree on the mixed pallet multi-drop route as first priority.
For the second, I would pick raw materials inbound because of the weight and the risk when we unload from the middle.
For special loads, maybe we can document both dangerous goods and animals later under T12, but for the first mapping I would keep it to one so we do not slow down.

From what I see on the floor, the biggest near misses are:
- Mixed pallet trucks where people walk into the forklift path to find a pallet.
- Raw materials where the floor is dirty and the load is very heavy.
I would support focusing on:
1) Mixed pallet multi-drop.
2) Raw materials inbound.
For special loads, animals are more visible and we already have some habits, while dangerous goods pictograms are often misunderstood.
Maybe we pick dangerous goods as the special case to map first, then add animals when we work on T12.

I am ok with starting on mixed pallet multi-drop and raw materials inbound.
Those are the ones where I see the most broken pallets and messy staging.
On special loads, I lean toward dangerous goods first because of the pictograms and the extra rules.
We can still note down what we do for animals so we do not forget it when we get to T12.

Sounds like we are converging.
Let me play it back to be sure we are aligned before I lock it into the T1 mapping and later into A5 for the pilot:
- Route 1: mixed pallet multi-drop outbound.
- Route 2: heavy raw materials inbound.
- Special load focus: dangerous goods, with animals noted for later.
If no one objects, I will treat this as our focus set for the first round of mapping and procedures.

No objection from me.
Those three cases cover most of my day.
Once you have the first draft of the T1 map, I can check if the steps match what we actually do when we are under time pressure.

Works for me as well.
When you share the T1 map, I will add any shortcuts I see people taking, especially around stacking and quick cleaning between trucks.

Agreed.
From the cleaning side, I will note what we currently do on those two routes so we can later compare with the new checklist and what we log in A5 during the pilot.

All good for me.
I will pay attention this week on raw materials trucks and note any unsafe stacking or cleaning gaps so we can feed that into T1.

Great, thanks all.
I will draft the current-state step list for those two routes plus dangerous goods and share a simple flow for review.
We will then be ready to move into drafting the SOP and guidelines.

threads.thread_goal: Review and finalise the draft SOP and stacking guideline before pilot.

messages.text:
I have pulled together a first version of the loading and unloading SOP and the stacking rules based on what we mapped in T1.
Summary:
- A1 covers pre-checks, loading, unloading and post-checks for the two main routes plus dangerous goods.
- A2 lists max layers and weight hints per pallet type, plus some examples for mixed loads.
- For special loads, I started a draft under T12 that will later feed into A6.
Can you all review with these questions in mind:
1) Are any key steps missing or out of order in A1?
2) Are the stacking limits in A2 realistic for what we see on the floor?
3) Anything unclear or too long for quick use on the dock?

I went through A1 quickly.
What I like:
- The pre-check on floor condition and dock plate is clear.
- The step about confirming route sequence before loading is good.
Questions:
- In the unloading section for raw materials, it says we should always start from the front of the trailer.
Sometimes we cannot reach the front first because of how the truck is parked.
Should we allow starting from the middle if we secure the load first?
On A2, the max layers for the blue pallets look a bit low compared to what we do now.
We often go one layer higher without issues, but maybe that is risky.
Not sure how strict we want to be for the pilot.

I read A1 and A2 as well.
On A1:
- The dangerous goods section mentions checking pictograms but does not say what to do if the label is damaged or missing.
Maybe add a step to stop and call the supervisor or safety officer.
On A2:
- The examples for mixed loads are helpful, but I would add one case where we have heavy boxes on light pallets stacked on top of stronger pallets.
That happens a lot.
For T2 and T3, I think the structure is good, but we might need a shorter quick-reference version for the dock wall later.

From the factory hand side, A1 looks workable.
The pre-checks and post-checks are clear enough that we can support movers.
One thing: the cleaning step after each truck might be too heavy if we do a full sweep every time.
Maybe we can define a quick between-truck clean and a deeper clean per shift.
On A2, I like that it mentions not stacking damaged pallets, but maybe we should say what to do with them: move to a repair or scrap area.
For T12 and A6, I can help later with the animal transport part when we get there.

I checked A2 in detail.
The weight hints per pallet type look reasonable from what I see on raw materials.
I agree with the comment that we sometimes go one layer higher today.
For the pilot, I would rather stay on the safe side and then adjust if it slows us down too much.
On A1, the step about coordinating with maintenance if equipment looks damaged is good, but maybe we should say to park the forklift out of use until checked.
That will avoid people using it anyway.

Thanks for the detailed reads.
Let me propose some tweaks based on your points:
- For raw materials unloading in A1, change the rule to: start from the front when reachable; if not, secure remaining load and then unload from the middle with extra care.
- For dangerous goods, add a step: if pictogram or label is damaged or missing, stop loading and call supervisor or safety officer.
- For cleaning, define two levels: quick between-truck clean and deeper per-shift clean.
- For A2 stacking limits, keep the conservative limits for the pilot, but add a note that we will review after we see data in A5.
Any objections to these changes before I update T2 and T3 drafts?

Those changes work for me.
The flexibility on unloading from the middle matches what we actually do, and the extra care note is a good reminder.
Keeping the stricter stacking limits for the pilot is fine as long as we really review them later with A5 data.

I am aligned with those tweaks.
Please also add that damaged labels on dangerous goods mean we do not move the pallet until someone with authority clears it.
On the quick vs deep clean, maybe we can later mirror that in the cleaning checklist A3 so it is consistent.

No objections.
The two-level cleaning approach will help us keep up with operations.
When we get to A3, we can spell out which items are between-truck and which are per-shift.
For A2, I like the idea of reviewing limits after the pilot using A5.

All good from my side.
Parking damaged forklifts out of use until checked should be clearly written in A1.
For T3, maybe add a simple visual in A2 showing good vs bad stacking on damaged pallets.
That will help people decide quickly.

I have now applied these changes to the T2 SOP draft and the T3 stacking guideline, and updated A1 and A2 accordingly.
Before we move to the pilot, we need to be clear that we are ok using these versions as our test standard.
To summarise what we would approve for the pilot:
- A1: includes flexible unloading rule, clear stop-and-call step for dangerous goods labels, and equipment out-of-use rule.
- A2: conservative stacking limits, damaged pallet rule, and mixed-load examples.
Are you comfortable treating A1 as the SOP for the pilot week and A2 as the stacking rules we will follow during that period?

Yes, I am ok using A1 as the SOP for the pilot.
The steps are clear enough that I can follow them even when it is busy.
For A2, I will stick to the limits during the pilot and note any cases where it really slows us down so we can log them in A5.

Same here, I am comfortable with A1 and A2 as pilot standards.
We just need to make sure everyone on shift has a quick way to see the key points, maybe a one-page summary later.
For now, I will follow A1 and A2 as written during the pilot.

Agreed from my side.
I will support movers in following A1 and A2 during the pilot and help capture any issues in A5.
Later, when we expand T12 and A6 for special loads, we can build on this base.

I am on board as well.
Using A1 and A2 consistently during the pilot will give us good data in A5 to decide if any limits can be relaxed without losing safety.
No further changes from me before the pilot.

Thanks all.
We will treat the current A1 as the approved SOP draft for the pilot and A2 as the stacking and weight distribution rules to apply.
I will freeze the T2 and T3 versions for the pilot and note any changes after we review A5.

threads.thread_goal: Define cleaning and inspection routines and how they will be tracked.

messages.text:
I have drafted a proposal for the new cleaning checklist and the tracking sheet.
- A3: daily loading bay cleaning and inspection list, split into between-truck quick tasks and per-shift deeper tasks.
- A8: simple tracker with date, shift, completed items and issues.
These are linked to T4 and T11.
Key points in A3:
- Floors and ramps: quick sweep between trucks if debris or spills, full sweep and spot clean once per shift.
- Equipment: visual check of forklifts and dock plates once per shift, note issues in A8.
- Emergency exits: check clear once per shift.
Please review and tell me if the tasks and timing look realistic for your shifts.

Thanks for putting this together.
On A3, the split between quick and per-shift tasks matches what we discussed in A1.
Questions from the mover side:
- For between-truck quick sweep, who is responsible if we are in the middle of a rush, mover or factory hand?
- For equipment visual checks, should we tie that to the first truck of each shift so it does not get forgotten?
On A8, I like the simple columns.
Maybe we should add a short free-text field for near-misses so we can later cross-check with A5 during the pilot.

Looking at A3 from my shift:
- Quick sweep between trucks is fine most of the time, but when we have three trucks waiting it will be hard to do more than push debris aside.
- The per-shift deep clean might be better placed at the end of the shift, not mid-shift.
On A8, I am ok filling it in, but it needs to be somewhere we pass by anyway, like near the time clock or the dock entrance.
Otherwise people will forget.

A3 looks good overall.
I would add a specific line for removing plastic wrap and broken boards from the dock edge.
That is one of our biggest trip hazards.
For A8, could we have a simple tick box for each shift to say: quick tasks done, deep tasks done, issues logged?
That way we do not have to write too much when it is busy.

From the factory hand side, the workload in A3 seems manageable if we spread tasks across shifts.
I suggest:
- Early shift: focus on ramps and exits.
- Late shift: deeper clean of staging areas.
On A8, I agree with placing it where everyone passes.
We could also use different pen colors per shift so it is easy to see who filled what.
For T11, that should still count as a simple tracking method.

Good points.
Proposal to refine A3 and A8:
- Responsibility: quick between-truck sweep done by whoever finishes the load, usually the mover, with factory hand stepping in when there is a queue.
- Equipment visual checks: tie them to the first truck of each shift, with a note in A3.
- Add explicit line for plastic wrap and broken boards removal.
- In A8, add tick boxes for quick and deep tasks, plus a short free-text field for near-misses.
We can mount A8 on a board near the dock entrance so everyone sees it.
Does this sound workable before we lock the checklist content?

Works for me.
Tying equipment checks to the first truck of the shift will make it easier to remember.
I can help remind movers during the first week.
Mounting A8 near the dock entrance is also good, we all pass there.

I am ok with that.
If quick sweep is on the mover who finishes the load, we just need to keep it really quick: push debris aside, pick up obvious hazards.
The deeper clean at end of shift can handle the rest.
Tick boxes in A8 will make it faster to fill.

Agreed.
Please make sure the plastic wrap and broken boards line in A3 is clear and visible.
On A8, maybe we can add a small note: if you tick issues, write at least one word in the near-miss field so we know what happened.

No concerns from me.
Splitting tasks by shift as I suggested and using A8 on the dock entrance board should keep it simple.
For T4, we will just need to print A3 and laminate it for clipboards.

Great, I will update A3 and A8 with these refinements and finalize T4 and T11 drafts.
Before we move on, we should confirm two things:
1) Are we ok approving the A3 checklist content as our standard for the pilot?
2) Do we agree that A8 on the dock entrance board is the place where each shift records completion and issues?
Once we confirm, I will prepare printed A3 copies and the A8 board.

From my side, yes to both.
A3 as you described is clear enough, and using A8 at the dock entrance will make it easy to keep up.
I will remind movers to tick and note near-misses during the pilot so we have good data for A5 later.

I am ok approving A3 as is and using A8 on the dock entrance board.
As long as the form is quick to fill, I will use it every shift.

Agreed on both points.
A3 content looks good for the pilot, and A8 at the dock entrance is the right spot.
No further changes from me.

Same here, I support approving A3 and using A8 as the central tracker.
I can help set up the board and explain it to the other factory hands.

Perfect, then we will go ahead with A3 as the approved checklist for the pilot and A8 as the place to record completion and issues each shift.
I will finalize T4 and T11, print A3 for clipboards, and set up the A8 board at the dock entrance.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and coordinate the one-week pilot on a selected dock.

messages.text:
Time to plan the one-week pilot.
Proposal:
- Pilot dock: Dock 2, since it handles both mixed pallet outbound and raw materials inbound.
- Pilot dates: next Monday to Sunday.
- Shifts: early and late shifts included, night shift only for cleaning and checks.
During the pilot we will use:
- A1 as the SOP.
- A2 as stacking rules.
- A3 and A8 for cleaning and tracking.
- A4 for route-based loading sequence.
We also need to agree how we log issues and incidents in A5 as part of T7.
Please share if Dock 2 and these shifts work for you, and how you suggest we handle logging in A5.

Dock 2 works for me, I am already there most days.
Early and late shifts are fine.
For A5 logging, maybe we can:
- Have one line per truck for any major issue.
- Add a simple code for type: S for safety, T for time delay, C for cleaning.
I can help fill A5 at the end of my shift if we keep it simple.

I am ok with Dock 2 and the dates.
One thought: on the first two days, maybe we should have someone more familiar with A1 and A2 on each shift to help others.
On A5, I like the idea of codes.
We could also note if the issue was related to loading sequence from A4 or to stacking from A2, so we know where to adjust.

From the factory hand side, Dock 2 is a good choice because we can control cleaning and high-risk zones better there.
Early and late shifts are covered.
For A5 logging, I suggest we:
- Use one sheet per day.
- At the bottom, have a short summary per shift of main issues.
That will make it easier to review T7 results later.

Dock 2 is fine for me as well.
I can support night shift with cleaning and making sure A3 and A8 are followed.
On A5, I like the idea of codes and daily sheets.
We should also note if the checklist A3 was fully completed or not for that day.

Good inputs.
Let me refine the pilot plan:
- Dock: 2.
- Dates: next Monday to Sunday.
- Shifts: early and late for full SOP use, night for cleaning and checks.
For A5 logging:
- One sheet per day.
- One line per truck with code S, T or C.
- Extra column to tag if issue is related to A1 steps, A2 stacking, A3 cleaning or A4 sequence.
- Short summary per shift at the bottom.
During T7, we will make sure every shift uses A5.
Any concerns with this setup before we confirm Dock 2 and the logging approach?

No concerns from me.
The codes and tags will help us see patterns quickly.
I will take care of filling A5 for the late shift on the first two days.

All good.
I can be the point person for A1 and A2 on the early shift for the first two days, helping others follow the new steps and record issues in A5.

I am aligned.
I will make sure A3 and A8 are in place at Dock 2 before the pilot starts and help night shift log cleaning-related issues in A5.

No issues from my side.
I will support with A3, A8 and A5 on night shift and make sure T7 conditions are met on our side.

Great, then we will lock in Dock 2 with early and late shifts for the one-week pilot starting next Monday, and use the A5 daily sheets with codes and tags as our logging method.
I will update T7 with these details and share the final pilot brief.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results, adjust documents and lock in training plan.

messages.text:
Pilot week on Dock 2 is complete.
I have summarized key findings from A5 and initial feedback from movers and drivers under T8.
Highlights:
- Turnaround time improved slightly on mixed pallet routes when A4 was followed.
- Fewer near-misses related to plastic wrap and broken boards, thanks to A3 and A8.
- Some complaints about conservative stacking limits in A2 slowing loading on very light goods.
We now need to:
1) Agree final tweaks to A1, A2, A3 based on T9.
2) Confirm the training walk-through content in A7 and T10.
3) Decide that these are our final versions going forward.
Please share any additional feedback from your shifts and what you think must change before we lock things in.

From my late shift experience:
- A1 worked well once we got used to it.
The pre-checks did not slow us down much.
- A2 was a bit strict for very light goods; we could probably allow one more layer there.
- A3 and A8 helped keep the dock cleaner, but sometimes we forgot to tick A8 when it was busy.
For A7 and T10, I think the training script should include one full example of loading a multi-drop truck using A4, so new people see how it flows.

On early shift:
- A1 dangerous goods steps were used twice; stopping for damaged labels worked well, but we had to wait for the supervisor.
- A2 stacking rules felt right for heavy goods, but for very light boxes we could safely go higher.
- A3 quick sweep between trucks made a big difference.
For T9, I would suggest:
- In A2, add a separate line for very light goods with a slightly higher layer limit.
- In A1, clarify who to call for dangerous goods issues so there is no confusion.
On A7, the training script is clear, but maybe we should add a short quiz or questions at the end of the walk-through.

From the cleaning and night shift side:
- A3 and A8 worked well once people got into the habit.
We saw fewer blocked exits and less debris.
- Some near-misses in A5 were still related to people walking through forklift paths, not cleaning.
For T9, I would keep A3 as is, maybe just bold the lines about exits and plastic wrap.
On A7 and T10, we should include a short part on housekeeping and how it links to safety, not just loading steps.

I agree with the points raised.
Looking at A5, most issues were tagged to stacking and route sequence early in the week, then dropped as people got used to A2 and A4.
For T9 adjustments:
- A2: add the lighter-goods exception with clear examples.
- A4: maybe add one more example route where we show how to handle last-minute changes.
On A7, I like the idea of a short quiz or at least asking people to repeat key do and dont items.

Thanks for the detailed feedback.
Based on A5 and your comments, here are the concrete changes I propose for T9:
- A1: clarify contact person for dangerous goods issues and keep the stop-and-call rule.
- A2: add a separate line for very light goods with one extra allowed layer, plus examples.
- A3: highlight exits and plastic wrap lines for visibility.
- A4: add an example for last-minute route changes.
For A7 and T10:
- Include a full multi-drop loading example using A4.
- Add a short Q and A at the end where the trainer asks about key steps and common mistakes.
If you agree, I will update the documents and the training script accordingly.

Those changes cover my concerns.
The lighter-goods exception in A2 will help a lot.
The training example in A7 using A4 will make it easier for new people to understand the sequence.
I am ok with you updating the docs as proposed.

Agreed.
Please make sure the dangerous goods contact in A1 is clear and does not change by shift.
On A7, the Q and A at the end is a good idea; we can keep it short but focused on the most common errors we saw in A5.

I am aligned with these updates.
Highlighting exits and plastic wrap in A3 will help keep attention on them.
In A7 and T10, please include one or two questions about housekeeping and walking paths, not only about forklifts and stacking.

No objections.
The proposed T9 changes reflect what we saw in A5.
For T10, we should also agree on a simple schedule so each shift gets the 15-minute walk-through within the next two weeks.

I have now applied the T9 updates to A1, A2, A3 and A4, and refreshed A7 with the new example and Q and A.
For T10, here is a simple training plan:
- Week 1: early shift walk-through on Monday and Wednesday, late shift on Tuesday and Thursday.
- Week 2: catch-up sessions for anyone who missed, plus night shift focus on cleaning and paths.
Each session uses A7 as the script and lasts about 15 minutes on the dock.
If we are all comfortable with the updated documents and this training schedule, we can treat them as final going forward.

The updated plan works for me.
The training slots fit our shift pattern and A7 is clear enough to follow.
I am ok treating A1, A2, A3 and A4 plus the A7 schedule as final.

Same here.
I will help run the early shift sessions using A7.
From my side, we can approve the final versions and the training schedule.

I am comfortable with the final documents and the training plan.
I will support the late and night shift sessions, focusing on A3 and walking paths.
Let us go ahead and roll this out.

Agreed.
The final A1, A2, A3, A4 and A7 reflect what worked in the pilot, and the T10 schedule is realistic.
I will help track completion of the sessions and note any further ideas in case we need a later refresh.

Thanks everyone.
We will treat the updated A1, A2, A3, A4 and A7 as our final standard documents and follow the agreed T10 training schedule.
I will close out T8 and T9 with a short summary and then we move into regular use and monitoring.
